name: EMA and the European AI Network
blurb: How European regulators are organising their own AI use.
title: EMA and the European AI Network
answer: The EMA and the national agencies coordinate AI through a network data steering group and publish an annual AI observatory report. The 2025 report described the year as the point where regulators' use of AI moved from adoption to practical application, while noting it records activity rather than setting requirements.

reading.body:
The EMA coordinates AI across European medicines regulators through a network steering group and an annual observatory report, which for 2025 described a shift from adoption to practical application.

The structure is coordination rather than regulation. A network data steering group and a yearly observatory are instruments for watching what national agencies do with AI, not for permitting or restricting it. The 2025 report is explicit that it records activity rather than setting requirements, so the document is a picture of practice, not a source of obligations.

For AI specifically, this matters because the evidence base for how regulators actually use these systems is thin. An observatory that aggregates activity across a network is one of the few public records of that use. It also sits alongside the EMA's September 2024 reflection paper on AI across the medicinal product lifecycle, which is the document that carries expectations for sponsors, including engaging the agency early through scientific advice when AI is central to evidence.

The data does not say which national agencies participate, what systems they run, or what the observatory found beyond the adoption-to-application framing. It does not connect this activity to compute, data centres, or power, and no such link should be inferred from it.

sections.body: Engage the EMA early through scientific advice when AI is central to evidence, as the reflection paper recommends.
